title: Review of Anatomy and Physiology of the Body Defence System
path: Review of Anatomy and Physiology of the Body Defence System

headings.title: Introduction to the Body Defence System
headings.content: The human body is constantly exposed to pathogenic microorganisms, toxins, and environmental antigens. To survive, the organism relies on the immune system, an intricate network of cells, tissues, and organs that recognize and neutralize foreign invaders. This defense architecture operates through two deeply integrated branches: innate immunity, which provides immediate, non-specific protection, and adaptive immunity, which mounts targeted, long-lasting responses complete with immunological memory. Maintaining homeostasis requires distinguishing self from non-self, preventing the immune system from launching destructive attacks against the host's own healthy tissues.

headings.title: Anatomy of Primary and Secondary Lymphoid Organs
headings.content:
Lymphoid organs are categorized by their role in lymphocyte development and activation.

- **Primary Lymphoid Organs**: The red bone marrow and the thymus gland. These sites support the production, maturation, and differentiation of B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes into immunocompetent cells.
- **Secondary Lymphoid Organs**: The lymph nodes, spleen, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), and tonsils. These structures trap antigens and provide an optimized physical environment where mature lymphocytes interact with foreign particles to initiate adaptive immune responses.

headings.title: Cells of the Immune System and Their Functions
headings.content:
All immune cells originate from pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells in the red bone marrow, differentiating into myeloid or lymphoid lineages.

| Cell Type | Lineage | Primary Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Neutrophil** | Myeloid | Rapid phagocytosis of bacteria during acute infection |
| **Macrophage** | Myeloid | Phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and tissue repair |
| **B-Lymphocyte** | Lymphoid | Differentiation into plasma cells to secrete antibodies |
| **Cytotoxic T-Cell** | Lymphoid | Induction of apoptosis in virus-infected or malignant cells |
| **Natural Killer Cell** | Lymphoid | Non-specific destruction of stressed or tumor-altered cells |

headings.title: Innate Immunity: Barriers and Non-Specific Responses
headings.content: Innate immunity requires no prior exposure to a pathogen. It comprises physical barriers like the stratified keratinized epithelium of the skin and the mucus membranes lining the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. Chemical barriers include the low pH of gastric secretions, lysozyme in tears, and antimicrobial peptides in sweat. If pathogens breach these structural lines, cellular components such as phagocytes and natural killer cells engage them immediately, relying on pattern recognition receptors to detect conserved molecular motifs unique to microbes.

headings.title: Adaptive Immunity: Humoral and Cell-Mediated Pathways
headings.content: When innate mechanisms are insufficient, the adaptive immune system engages through two cooperative arms. Humoral immunity centers on extracellular pathogens and relies on B-cells producing soluble antibodies that neutralize toxins or opsonize microbes for destruction. Cell-mediated immunity handles intracellular pathogens, such as viruses and certain bacteria, utilizing T-lymphocytes. Helper T-cells coordinate the overall immune response by releasing cytokines, while cytotoxic T-cells physically bind to and destroy infected host cells. Both pathways generate memory cells, ensuring a rapid, robust defense upon subsequent encounters with the identical antigen.

headings.title: The Complement System and Inflammatory Response
headings.content: The complement system consists of a cascade of plasma proteins synthesized primarily by the liver, circulating in an inactive state. Upon encountering pathogen surfaces, these proteins activate sequentially via classical, lectin, or alternative pathways. This activation triggers opsonization, leukocyte chemotaxis, and the formation of membrane attack complexes that punch holes in microbial cell membranes. Concurrently, localized tissue injury or infection prompts an acute inflammatory response. Vasodilation and increased capillary permeability allow plasma proteins and phagocytes to exit the bloodstream, producing classic signs of heat, redness, swelling, and pain while walling off the affected area.

headings.title: Physiological Regulation and Immune Tolerance
headings.content: Unchecked immune activity can lead to widespread tissue destruction and autoimmune disease. Immune tolerance is the mechanism by which the body prevents self-reactive lymphocytes from attacking host tissues. Central tolerance occurs in primary lymphoid organs, where developing T and B cells that strongly recognize self-antigens undergo apoptosis. Peripheral tolerance mechanisms operate in secondary lymphoid organs, suppressing rogue lymphocytes through regulatory T-cells and clonal anergy. Regulatory T-cells secrete suppressive cytokines, dampening immune responses once an infection has been successfully cleared and preventing chronic inflammation.

headings.title: Clinical Relevance for Nursing Practice in Nigeria
headings.content: Understanding immune physiology is vital for nursing practice in Nigeria, where infectious diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV heavily impact population health. Persistent parasitic infections like Plasmodium species modulate host immune responses, altering phagocytic clearance and predisposing patients to secondary bacterial infections. Malnutrition, frequently encountered in resource-limited settings, compromises primary and secondary lymphoid organ integrity, leading to impaired lymphocyte proliferation and reduced antibody titers. Nurses must recognize how physiological deficits in immune defense translate to clinical vulnerability, guiding targeted interventions in wound care, nutritional support, and vaccination campaigns.
